package_info.package_manager: N/A (malicious document, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: The Excel document is weaponized with a VBA macro that initiates a multi-stage malware chain, ultimately deploying Cobalt Strike. It leverages obfuscated payloads, anti-analysis checks, geo-fencing, persistence via registry autorun, process injection, and encrypted C2 communication to compromise Windows systems and establish remote attacker control.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drop HEX-encoded DLL as 'Ac83faafb23919Ae9.DLl' into '%APPDATA%\VIBErpc\bIn\biN'; create shortcut 'ACtIVePRObE.lnk' in '%APPDATA%\Microsoft'; execute 'RunDLL32.EXE shell32.dll,ShellExec_RunDLL "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\ACtIVePRObE.lnk", 0' to trigger DLL via regsvr32.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user enables macros, the code decodes a HEX-encoded DLL, writes it to disk, creates a shortcut, and executes it via RunDLL32 and regsvr32, resulting in the launch of the next malware stage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing DLLs from Office macros is a well-known malware tactic. The use of encoded payloads, non-standard file paths, and indirect execution via LNK and regsvr32 is designed to evade static and behavioral detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Excel macros should not write or execute binary files, especially using obfuscated payloads and indirect execution methods.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some business macros automate document workflows, but they do not deploy or execute DLLs or create shortcuts for binary execution.
key_indicators: HEX-encoded DLL payloads in macro code
DLL dropped to uncommon subdirectory in %APPDATA%
Creation and execution of LNK shortcut to launch DLL
Abuse of regsvr32 for DLL execution

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated .NET DLL checks for analysis/AV processes ('processhacker', 'avastui', etc.), terminates if found; if not, downloads payload from 'hxxps://goudieelectric[.]shop/cms/svg/6364.2809640e[.]chunk.svg' (Ukraine-only); extracts base64 data, XOR-decodes, writes to TEMP, executes via rundll32.exe, deletes after execution.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon DLL execution, the code enumerates running processes for analysis or AV tools, terminates if detected, otherwise downloads a geo-fenced payload, decodes and writes it to TEMP, executes it via rundll32.exe, and deletes the payload after execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process enumeration for security tools, geo-fenced payload delivery, and self-deletion are advanced evasion and anti-analysis techniques. Downloading and executing code from an external domain is a hallmark of staged malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not terminate AV or analysis tools, download code from suspicious domains, or self-delete after execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Geo-fencing is used in some region-locked software, but not for downloading and executing code in this manner.
key_indicators: Process enumeration for known AV/analysis tools
Conditional payload download based on geolocation
Obfuscated network communication to external domain

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Decrypts next-stage payload using RC4, writes to 'C:\ProgramData\Windows\Containers\BaseImages\...\ResetEngine.dll'; adds persistence via registry key 'SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' with value 'regsvr32.exe /s ...ResetEngine.dll'; executes via InvokeMethod.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code decrypts the next-stage payload using RC4, writes the DLL to a system directory, creates a registry autorun key for persistence, and executes the DLL using reflection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: RC4 decryption of payloads, writing to obscure system paths, and establishing persistence via registry autorun are classic malware techniques to evade detection and maintain access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not decrypt and drop DLLs to system folders or create autorun registry keys for regsvr32 to execute non-standard DLLs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Registry autorun is used by some legitimate updaters, but not for executing DLLs in this manner or from these locations.
key_indicators: DLL written to deep system directory
Registry autorun key for regsvr32 with suspicious DLL

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Uses NtDelayExecution for sandbox evasion; inspects and terminates parent process (anti-debugging); decrypts final payload with AES; injects into self and uses APIs (GetCurrentProcessId, OpenProcess, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread, WaitForSingleObject) to execute Cobalt Strike Beacon.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the DLL delays execution to evade sandboxes, checks and terminates its parent process for anti-debugging, decrypts the Cobalt Strike payload using AES, and injects it into memory using process injection APIs, resulting in in-memory execution of the Beacon.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Delaying execution, anti-debugging checks, AES decryption, and process injection are advanced techniques used to evade detection and analysis, and to execute malicious payloads in memory.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not perform process injection, terminate parent processes, or use anti-analysis tricks such as delayed execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Process injection APIs are used in some legitimate debuggers or performance tools, but not in this context or with these behaviors.
key_indicators: Use of process injection APIs (VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Beacon configuration XORed with 0x2E; C2 URLs: 'hxxps://simonandschuster[.]shop/the-zero-residual-concept/products' and 'hxxps://simonandschuster[.]shop/the-zero-residual-concept/sjj-solutions'; establishes C2 communication.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Beacon decodes its configuration using XOR, retrieves C2 URLs, and establishes encrypted command-and-control communication with attacker infrastructure, enabling remote access and control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Cobalt Strike is a widely abused post-exploitation tool. XOR-obfuscated configuration and encrypted C2 communication are used to evade detection and enable remote attacker control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate software should beacon to these C2 domains or use Cobalt Strike Beacon shellcode.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encrypted network communication is common in legitimate software, but not to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure or with obfuscated configs.
key_indicators: Encrypted C2 traffic to attacker domains

attack_chain.action: User opens Excel document and enables macros, triggering VBA code.
VBA macro decodes, drops, and executes an obfuscated DLL downloader.
DLL downloader checks for analysis tools, applies geo-fencing, downloads the next stage payload, decodes and executes it, and deletes traces.
Next-stage DLL decrypts payload, writes to disk, establishes persistence via registry autorun, and executes the payload.
ResetEngine.dll delays execution, evades analysis, decrypts and injects Cobalt Strike Beacon into memory.
Cobalt Strike Beacon decodes configuration and establishes encrypted C2 communication.

behavioral_signatures: Office macro decodes and drops DLLs to disk
Obfuscated or encoded payloads embedded in macro code
DLLs that enumerate and terminate AV or analysis tools
Geo-fenced payload delivery based on system locale or IP
Registry autorun keys referencing regsvr32.exe with non-standard DLLs
Process injection and in-memory execution of payloads
Delayed execution and anti-debugging routines (e.g., NtDelayExecution)
AES or RC4 decryption of embedded payloads
Cobalt Strike Beacon configuration obfuscated with XOR
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents that decode and drop DLLs, especially via encoded macros. Detect creation of registry autorun keys referencing regsvr32.exe and DLLs in non-standard locations. Alert on process injection APIs and delayed execution routines in DLLs. Flag outbound connections to known C2 domains and geo-fenced payload downloads. Use YARA rules for encoded payloads, RC4/AES decryption routines, and Cobalt Strike Beacon signatures. Correlate file, process, and network activity for multi-stage attack patterns.
